questions.original_question: Do rising debt burdens increase the probability of a subsequent systemic banking crisis?
questions.current_answer: H01-P1.0 found no predictive value in 5-year public-debt/GDP growth before banking crises (AUC 0.30-0.38); public and private debt behave differently around banking crises.

available_datasets.role: BIS sectoral credit (govt, private, household, corporate) & policy rates

missing_datasets.reason: official ZIP HTTP 403/404; local-file importer ready

historical_coverage.achieved: 1870-2020 retrospective JST R6 + BIS sectoral credit 1947-2026Q1

supporting_evidence: A complete leakage-aware protocol was registered and executed.
Diagnostic contrast shows private bank-loan/GDP 5y growth (tloans/gdp) reaches retrospective AUC 0.721 (1y) and 0.702 (2y), confirming public vs private debt must never be conflated.
contradictory_evidence: Registered H01-P1.0 tested public debtgdp 5-year change: held-out AUC was 0.363 (1y), 0.381 (2y), 0.296 (5y) and top-p80 precision (1.54%/1.50%/0.88%) fell below the ~3.42% base rate because public debt typically surges after banking crises rather than before them.
alternative_explanations: Pre-crisis private credit booms improve fiscal balances before banking crises, while public debt surges post-crisis via bailouts and automatic stabilisers.
questions.falsification_criteria: No improvement over the unconditional base rate or discrimination near/below random ordering is evidence inconsistent with predictive value.
scientific_limitations: H01-P1.0 evaluated public debtgdp rather than private tloans/gdp; protocol is preserved unchanged.
13 of 19 post-1990 test events cluster in 2007-2008 and 4 in 1991.
Secular post-1990 debt drift pushed 35.1%-40.8% of test rows above the pre-1990 80th percentile.

source_references.label: Ray Dalio, Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order

questions.original_question: Does rapid private credit expansion precede financial crises independently of income growth?
questions.current_answer: Preserved contradictory H01-P1.0 benchmark reflects a variable mismatch (public debtgdp was tested instead of private tloans/gdp); exploratory tloans/gdp shows positive retrospective association but awaits an independent pre-registered protocol.

available_datasets.role: BIS sectoral credit (govt, private, household, corporate) & policy rates

supporting_evidence: In diagnostic inspection on the 1990-2020 JST holdout, 5-year private bank-loan/GDP change (tloans/gdp) yields retrospective AUC 0.721 (1y), 0.702 (2y), 0.590 (5y).
contradictory_evidence: The sole pre-registered evaluation (H01-P1.0) tested public debtgdp 5-year change rather than private tloans/gdp and failed (AUC 0.363/0.381/0.296); no separate private-credit protocol controlling for income growth and global crisis clustering has been pre-registered.
alternative_explanations: Credit growth can reflect financial deepening, denominator contractions or synchronized global credit waves (13/19 test crises occurred in 2007-2008).
questions.falsification_criteria: A registered test must fail to outperform its declared baseline or produce no independent evidence.
scientific_limitations: Contradictory status is preserved from H01-P1.0 because H01-P1.0 may not be rewritten ex-post; a dedicated private-credit protocol must be registered separately and tested against independent post-cutoff data.

supporting_evidence: Military spending is explicitly labelled a resource proxy, not capability.
contradictory_evidence: No capability or transition outcomes exist for evaluation.
alternative_explanations: Technology, alliances, geography and readiness can dominate spending.
questions.falsification_criteria: A registered test must fail to outperform its declared baseline or produce no independent evidence.

source_references.label: Ray Dalio, Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order

questions.original_question: Do international banking and financial-centre activity predict monetary or financial influence?
questions.current_answer: Unanswered with the current Atlas evidence.

available_datasets.role: BIS cross-border bank claims by currency and reporting jurisdiction
BIS Triennial FX turnover shares 1989-2025 (including INR)

available_datasets.dataset: listed-market capitalisation, private credit, broad money

historical_coverage.achieved: BIS LBS cross-border banking 1977Q4-2026Q2 + BIS FX turnover 1989-2025 + modern domestic depth

country_coverage.achieved: 8 primary countries + global BIS reporting total

existing_research_methods: domestic market depth separated from cross-border banking intermediation
supporting_evidence: BIS LBS shows UK leads cross-border banking share (14.3% in 2026Q2) while US leads equity market cap, demonstrating why stock-market cap/GDP is an incomplete financial-centre measure.
contradictory_evidence: No independent financial-influence outcome labels exist for predictive testing.
alternative_explanations: Financial influence may depend on legal jurisdiction, clearing infrastructure, currency networks and capital-account openness.
questions.falsification_criteria: A registered test must fail to outperform its declared baseline or produce no independent evidence.

source_references.label: Ray Dalio, Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order

questions.original_question: Can concentration or multipolarity in power measures be quantified without a universal national power score?
questions.current_answer: Unanswered with the current Atlas evidence.

available_datasets.role: official FX reserve shares & claims (1995-2026Q2; currency-level)
BIS cross-border bank claims by currency and reporting jurisdiction

missing_datasets.dataset: registered HHI/shares method across complete global universe

historical_coverage.achieved: modern denominator-safe global shares + currency/banking denominators

supporting_evidence: The design explicitly avoids a manufactured national power score.
contradictory_evidence: Concentration across only 8 tracked countries cannot compute a full global Herfindahl index without rest-of-world country shares.
alternative_explanations: Different dimensions imply different concentration patterns (e.g. multipolar PPP GDP vs concentrated USD FX/reserve role).
questions.falsification_criteria: A registered test must fail to outperform its declared baseline or produce no independent evidence.

questions.original_question: Do productivity and human-capital measures predict long-run economic resilience?
questions.current_answer: Unanswered with the current Atlas evidence.

available_datasets.role: Penn World Table 11.0 output, worker/hour productivity, capital, human capital & TFP (1950-2023)

historical_coverage.achieved: PWT 11.0 (1950-2023 real GDP, worker/hour productivity, capital, hc, ctfp/rtfpna) + OECD 1970-2025

existing_research_methods: separate PWT 2021 PPP, PWT constant national-accounts and OECD-relative productivity definitions
supporting_evidence: PWT 11.0 real GDP, GDP per worker, GDP per hour (where hours exist), capital stock, human capital index and TFP are imported without combining incompatible PPP bases.
contradictory_evidence: No independent long-run resilience outcome test exists.
alternative_explanations: Resilience may reflect macro buffers, institutions or external demand rather than measured human capital alone.
